passages.title: The Preacher asks what work gains
passages.summary: These are the words of the Preacher, a son of David and king in Jerusalem. He says everything is vapor. He asks what people gain from all their work under the sun. Generations come and go, and the earth stays. The sun rises and sets, and rivers run to a sea that never fills. Nothing is new, and earlier people are forgotten. He set his mind to study all that is done. He found that much wisdom brings much grief.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies what gives temporary life lasting value. Why does the Preacher compare human work with wind and rivers?

contextNote.title: Repeated cycles question the promise of lasting gain
contextNote.text: Verse 3 asks what “profit” a person has from work. The word asks what is left over at the end. Verses 4–7 give four examples of motion with no gain. Generations, sun, wind, and rivers all return to where they began. Verse 9 draws the conclusion that nothing is new. Verse 11 adds that people forget what came before. “Under the sun” marks this as a report of life as observed.

passages.title: Pleasure and great works do not last
passages.summary: The Preacher tests pleasure, laughter, and wine. He builds houses, plants vineyards, and makes gardens and pools. He gathers servants, herds, silver, gold, and singers. He denies himself nothing his eyes want. Then he looks at it all and finds it empty. Wisdom is better than folly, yet the wise and the fool both die. He hates his work, since he must leave it to someone else. He concludes that enjoying food and work is a gift from God.
passages.uncertainty: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies mortal life as temporary. Why does leaving his work to another person trouble the Preacher?

contextNote.title: Inheritance interrupts achievement
contextNote.text: The Preacher finishes more than anyone before him (verse 9). Verse 18 names what spoils it. He must leave it all to the next man. Verse 19 says no one knows whether that heir will be wise or a fool. Verse 21 adds that the heir did not work for it. First Kings 12 shows Solomon’s son losing most of a kingdom. Verse 24 turns from gain to gift: enjoyment comes from God’s hand.

passages.title: Changing times and shared death
passages.summary: The Preacher says everything has its season. There is a time to be born and to die, to weep and to laugh. There is a time for war and a time for peace. God has made everything beautiful in its time. He has put eternity in human hearts. Yet people cannot find out all that God does. Injustice sits where justice should be, and people die as animals do. The best a person can do is rejoice and do good.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies wisdom while recognizing life’s limits. Why does the Preacher connect enjoyment of work with what people cannot know?

contextNote.title: A list of times does not grant control
contextNote.text: The poem in verses 1–8 lists fourteen pairs of times. People do not choose most of them. Birth, death, war, and loss arrive on their own schedule. Verse 11 names two gifts that pull against each other. Each thing is fitting in its time, and people sense something lasting. They still cannot see the whole work from start to finish. So verses 12–13 advise taking present good as a gift.

passages.title: Power, lonely work, and companions
passages.summary: The Preacher looks at the oppression done under the sun. The oppressed weep and have no one to comfort them. He sees that much hard work comes from envy of a neighbor. One handful with quiet is better than two with toil. A man works alone with no son or brother and never asks for whom. Two are better than one, for one can lift the other. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken. A poor, wise youth is better than an old, foolish king.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: What does a companion provide that the lonely worker’s wealth cannot?

contextNote.title: Observation exposes the limits of private advice
contextNote.text: Verse 1 reports what the Preacher “saw.” He says twice that the oppressed had no comforter. Power stood on the side of those who harmed them. He offers no remedy and does not look away. Verses 9–12 give a partial answer on a small scale. A companion lifts the one who falls and keeps him warm. That is the comfort verse 1 found missing.

passages.title: Listen before making promises
passages.summary: The Preacher says to guard your steps at God’s house. It is better to listen than to offer a fool’s sacrifice. God is in heaven, so words should be few. A vow to God must be paid without delay. It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Whoever loves money never has enough. A worker sleeps well, and a rich man’s plenty keeps him awake. To enjoy food and work is God’s gift.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher prefer making no promise to leaving one unpaid?

contextNote.title: Words before God create obligations
contextNote.text: Verses 1–2 set the scene: come to listen, and say little. A vow was freely made; no one had to make it (Deuteronomy 23:21–23). Verse 4 says that once spoken, it is owed. Verse 5 prefers no vow to a broken one. Verse 6 pictures a person telling the temple messenger it was a mistake. Words spoken before God have weight. The Preacher’s caution about speech runs through verses 3 and 7 as well.

passages.title: Having wealth without enjoying it
passages.summary: The Preacher describes a heavy misfortune he has seen. God gives a man riches and honor, and he lacks nothing. Yet God does not let him enjoy them, and a stranger does. A man might have a hundred children and live long. If he finds no good in life, a stillborn child is better off. All a person’s work is for his mouth, and his appetite is never filled. What the eyes see is better than restless desire. No one knows what is good for a person in his few days.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the wealthy person’s experience challenge measuring life by possessions?

contextNote.title: Possession and enjoyment can separate
contextNote.text: Chapter 5:19 said the power to enjoy wealth is a gift from God. Verse 2 shows a case where that gift is missing. The man has everything and tastes none of it. So having and enjoying are two separate things. A stranger ends up with what he gathered. Verse 9 commends being content with what is in front of you. The chapter ends in questions (verse 12) and gives no rule.

passages.title: Mourning and unfair outcomes
passages.summary: A good name is better than fine perfume. A house of mourning is better to visit than a house of feasting. A wise person’s rebuke is better than the song of fools. Do not ask why the old days were better. In good times be glad, and in bad times consider that God made both. The Preacher has seen the righteous die young and the wicked live long. No one on earth is so righteous that he never sins. God made people upright, and they have looked for many schemes.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why does the Preacher think a house of mourning can teach the living?

contextNote.title: A funeral teaches what amusement can conceal
contextNote.text: Verse 2 compares two houses. A feast lets people forget how life ends. A funeral shows “the end of all men.” The verse says the living should take that to heart. Its aim is clear sight, not gloom. Verse 14 adds that good days and bad days both come from God. Verse 15 reports a case that breaks the expected rule, as Job’s does.

passages.title: A ruler’s power and delayed justice
passages.summary: Wisdom makes a person’s face shine. The Preacher advises obeying the king, whose word has power. No one has power over the wind or over the day of death. When a sentence for wrong is slow, people grow bold in doing evil. He says it will go well with those who fear God. Yet the righteous sometimes get what the wicked deserve. The wicked sometimes get what the righteous deserve. So he commends joy, and he admits no one can grasp all that God does.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does delayed punishment affect the people who watch wrongdoing?

contextNote.title: Observed injustice strains a familiar rule
contextNote.text: Verses 12–13 state what he knows: it goes well with those who fear God. Verse 14 states what he sees. Good people sometimes receive what bad people have earned. He sets the two statements side by side. He does not give up either one. Verse 11 notes what delayed justice does to those who watch. Verse 17 ends by admitting the limits of what anyone can find out.

passages.title: Death, chance, and forgotten wisdom
passages.summary: The righteous and the wise are in God’s hand. One fate comes to everyone, and a living dog is better than a dead lion. So eat your bread with joy and enjoy life with the wife you love. Do with your strength whatever your hand finds to do. The race does not always go to the swift. Time and chance happen to all. A poor wise man once saved a small city from a great king. Afterward no one remembered him.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Why do the poor man’s useful words fail to bring him lasting honor?

contextNote.title: Useful wisdom can remain unrecognized
contextNote.text: The story in verses 14–15 takes three sentences. A great king besieges a small town. A poor man’s wisdom saves it. Then no one remembers him. His wisdom worked, and his reward failed. Verse 16 still says wisdom is better than strength. Its worth does not depend on being noticed.

passages.title: Small mistakes and careless rulers
passages.summary: A few dead flies spoil a jar of perfume, and a little folly outweighs wisdom. Fools are set in high places while the able sit low. Whoever digs a pit may fall into it. Whoever splits logs may be hurt by them. A dull ax needs more strength, and skill brings success. A fool talks without end. Woe to a land whose rulers feast in the morning. Do not curse the king even in your thoughts.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: How does the blunt axe show the value of preparing before work?

contextNote.title: Skill matters within a fragile world
contextNote.text: Verses 8–9 say ordinary work carries risk. Digging, breaking walls, and cutting stone or wood can all injure. Verse 10 shows where wisdom helps. A sharpened ax needs less force. Preparing first saves strength later. The claim is modest: skill gives an advantage, not a guarantee. Verse 11 adds a case where help comes too late.

passages.title: Act without knowing every outcome
passages.summary: The Preacher says to send your bread out on the water. Give shares to seven or eight, since you do not know what trouble may come. Whoever watches the wind will not sow. Whoever studies the clouds will not reap. No one knows the way of the wind or how bones form in the womb. So sow in the morning and keep working in the evening. Light is sweet, and a person should enjoy all his years. The young should rejoice and remember that God will judge.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Scripture Helps connects bread on water with giving without expecting immediate repayment. Why does the Preacher tell the worker to sow in morning and evening?

contextNote.title: Uncertainty can become an excuse for inaction
contextNote.text: Verse 4 pictures a farmer waiting for perfect weather. He watches the sky and never plants. The chapter says “you don’t know” four times (verses 2, 5, 6). The Preacher does not treat that as a reason to wait. He treats it as a reason to act widely. Give to seven or eight, and sow morning and evening. Uncertainty is an argument for doing more.

passages.title: Remember your Creator before old age
passages.summary: The Preacher says to remember your Creator while you are young. Hard days will come when the sun and light grow dim. The guards of the house tremble, and the grinders are few. The windows darken, and the doors are shut. People go to their lasting home, and mourners walk the streets. The dust returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to God. The Preacher taught the people and chose his words with care. The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments.
passages.uncertainty: The example does not name a secure map location.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects lasting value with fearing God and keeping his commands. What does remembering the Creator change before the losses described in this chapter?

contextNote.title: The ending places limits around learning
contextNote.text: Verses 2–7 describe old age as a house falling into decline. In verses 9–10 the closing writer speaks about the Preacher. He praises him for weighing and arranging his sayings. Verse 11 compares wise words to goads and firmly set nails. Verse 12 warns that books have no end and study tires the body. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows writing tools from that wider world. Verses 13–14 give the limit that matters: fear God, who judges every deed.

words.label: Scribes
words.meaning: People trained to write and to keep records. In the Gospels, scribes also teach the law.

words.label: Assembly
words.meaning: A gathering of people. In the New Testament letters it means a group of believers. Many translations say “church.”

guides.title: Ecclesiastes: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Repeated cycles question the promise of lasting gain
steps.text: Verse 3 asks what “profit” a person has from work. The word asks what is left over at the end. Verses 4–7 give four examples of motion with no gain. Generations, sun, wind, and rivers all return to where they began. Verse 9 draws the conclusion that nothing is new. Verse 11 adds that people forget what came before. “Under the sun” marks this as a report of life as observed.

steps.title: Observation exposes the limits of private advice
steps.text: Verse 1 reports what the Preacher “saw.” He says twice that the oppressed had no comforter. Power stood on the side of those who harmed them. He offers no remedy and does not look away. Verses 9–12 give a partial answer on a small scale. A companion lifts the one who falls and keeps him warm. That is the comfort verse 1 found missing.

steps.title: The ending places limits around learning
steps.text: Verses 2–7 describe old age as a house falling into decline. In verses 9–10 the closing writer speaks about the Preacher. He praises him for weighing and arranging his sayings. Verse 11 compares wise words to goads and firmly set nails. Verse 12 warns that books have no end and study tires the body. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows writing tools from that wider world. Verses 13–14 give the limit that matters: fear God, who judges every deed.

chapterMaps.note: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.
chapterMaps.narrative: These are the words of the Preacher, a son of David and king in Jerusalem. He says everything is vapor. He asks what people gain from all their work under the sun. Generations come and go, and the earth stays. The sun rises and sets, and rivers run to a sea that never fills. Nothing is new, and earlier people are forgotten. He set his mind to study all that is done. He found that much wisdom brings much grief.
chapterMaps.limits: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.

chapterMaps.note: Jerusalem supplies the opening speaker’s setting.
chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher tests pleasure, laughter, and wine. He builds houses, plants vineyards, and makes gardens and pools. He gathers servants, herds, silver, gold, and singers. He denies himself nothing his eyes want. Then he looks at it all and finds it empty. Wisdom is better than folly, yet the wise and the fool both die. He hates his work, since he must leave it to someone else. He concludes that enjoying food and work is a gift from God.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher says everything has its season. There is a time to be born and to die, to weep and to laugh. There is a time for war and a time for peace. God has made everything beautiful in its time. He has put eternity in human hearts. Yet people cannot find out all that God does. Injustice sits where justice should be, and people die as animals do. The best a person can do is rejoice and do good.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher looks at the oppression done under the sun. The oppressed weep and have no one to comfort them. He sees that much hard work comes from envy of a neighbor. One handful with quiet is better than two with toil. A man works alone with no son or brother and never asks for whom. Two are better than one, for one can lift the other. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken. A poor, wise youth is better than an old, foolish king.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher says to guard your steps at God’s house. It is better to listen than to offer a fool’s sacrifice. God is in heaven, so words should be few. A vow to God must be paid without delay. It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Whoever loves money never has enough. A worker sleeps well, and a rich man’s plenty keeps him awake. To enjoy food and work is God’s gift.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher describes a heavy misfortune he has seen. God gives a man riches and honor, and he lacks nothing. Yet God does not let him enjoy them, and a stranger does. A man might have a hundred children and live long. If he finds no good in life, a stillborn child is better off. All a person’s work is for his mouth, and his appetite is never filled. What the eyes see is better than restless desire. No one knows what is good for a person in his few days.

chapterMaps.narrative: A good name is better than fine perfume. A house of mourning is better to visit than a house of feasting. A wise person’s rebuke is better than the song of fools. Do not ask why the old days were better. In good times be glad, and in bad times consider that God made both. The Preacher has seen the righteous die young and the wicked live long. No one on earth is so righteous that he never sins. God made people upright, and they have looked for many schemes.

chapterMaps.narrative: Wisdom makes a person’s face shine. The Preacher advises obeying the king, whose word has power. No one has power over the wind or over the day of death. When a sentence for wrong is slow, people grow bold in doing evil. He says it will go well with those who fear God. Yet the righteous sometimes get what the wicked deserve. The wicked sometimes get what the righteous deserve. So he commends joy, and he admits no one can grasp all that God does.

chapterMaps.narrative: The righteous and the wise are in God’s hand. One fate comes to everyone, and a living dog is better than a dead lion. So eat your bread with joy and enjoy life with the wife you love. Do with your strength whatever your hand finds to do. The race does not always go to the swift. Time and chance happen to all. A poor wise man once saved a small city from a great king. Afterward no one remembered him.

chapterMaps.narrative: A few dead flies spoil a jar of perfume, and a little folly outweighs wisdom. Fools are set in high places while the able sit low. Whoever digs a pit may fall into it. Whoever splits logs may be hurt by them. A dull ax needs more strength, and skill brings success. A fool talks without end. Woe to a land whose rulers feast in the morning. Do not curse the king even in your thoughts.

chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher says to send your bread out on the water. Give shares to seven or eight, since you do not know what trouble may come. Whoever watches the wind will not sow. Whoever studies the clouds will not reap. No one knows the way of the wind or how bones form in the womb. So sow in the morning and keep working in the evening. Light is sweet, and a person should enjoy all his years. The young should rejoice and remember that God will judge.

chapterMaps.note: The example does not name a secure map location.
chapterMaps.narrative: The Preacher says to remember your Creator while you are young. Hard days will come when the sun and light grow dim. The guards of the house tremble, and the grinders are few. The windows darken, and the doors are shut. People go to their lasting home, and mourners walk the streets. The dust returns to the earth, and the spirit returns to God. The Preacher taught the people and chose his words with care. The conclusion is to fear God and keep his commandments.
